1.title: The Three-Tier Structure at a Glance
1.html:
The Alsace AOC system has a clear three-tier structure — the more specific the name, the stricter the rules and the lower the yield limits:

① Alsace (Vin d'Alsace) — base tier
Covers the whole delimited area, about 74% of Alsace's total output. Lees ageing of more than 12 months is required, with a base yield limit of 80 hl/ha (plus a 20% flexible PLC limit). White and rosé can be made; varieties include Riesling, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois and Chardonnay (Crémant only); rosé may be made only from Pinot Noir.
② Alsace + Geographical Denomination (Dénomination géographique) — middle tier
After the name "Alsace", one of 13 officially recognised geographical names may be added: Bergheim, Blienschwiller, Coteaux du Haut-Koenigsbourg, Côtes de Barr, Côte de Rouffach, Klevener de Heiligenstein, Ottrott, Rodern, Saint-Hippolyte, Scherwiller, Vallée Noble, Val Saint-Grégoire, Wolxheim — each denomination is limited to specific villages and has its own authorised varieties.
③ Alsace Grand Cru — top tier
Named after a single delimited site (lieu-dit), only about 4% of the region's output. In principle it must come from a single noble variety (one of Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris or Muscat) and be hand-harvested. The base yield is only 55 hl/ha (PLC up to 66 hl/ha) — about 30% lower than the base Alsace tier.
2.title: Examples of Denominations and Their Authorised Varieties
2.html:
Each geographical denomination has its own limited authorised varieties — which is exactly what makes it "more specific, stricter":

DenominationAuthorised varieties
Scherwiller, WolxheimRiesling
Blienschwiller, Côtes de BarrSylvaner
Ottrott, Rodern, Saint-HippolytePinot Noir (red)
Klevener de HeiligensteinSavagnin rose (non-aromatic Gewurztraminer variant)
Côte de Rouffach, Vallée NobleGewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Riesling
3.title: The Two Blending Exceptions
3.html:
Alsace Grand Cru in principle comes from a single noble variety, but two long-established exceptions allow blends:

Altenberg de Bergheim: a blend of 50–70% Riesling, 10–25% Pinot Gris and 10–25% Gewurztraminer
Kaefferkopf (Ammerschwihr): a blend of 60–80% Gewurztraminer, 10–40% Riesling and up to 30% Pinot Gris

These two Grand Crus are also the only ones that do not need to (and usually do not) show a single variety name on the label.
4.question: Which of the following correctly describes the three-tier Alsace AOC structure?
4.options.0: Alsace Grand Cru has the highest share of output, about 74% of the region
4.options.1: From bottom to top the tiers are Alsace (base) → Alsace + geographical denomination (middle) → Alsace Grand Cru (top); the more specific the name, the stricter the rules and the lower the yield limit
4.options.2: The geographical-denomination tier has no variety restriction; any variety may be used
4.options.3: Grand Cru allows any variety to be blended with no restrictions at all
4.explanation: From bottom to top, the three tiers of the Alsace AOC are: Alsace (base tier, about 74% of output, base yield 80 hl/ha), Alsace + geographical denomination (13 recognised names, each limiting the authorised varieties) and Alsace Grand Cru (top tier, only about 4% of output, base yield only 55 hl/ha). The more specific the name, the stricter the rules and the lower the maximum yield — the core of the classification logic.
5.keyPoints.0: Three tiers: Alsace (base, 74% of output) → + geographical denomination (13) → Alsace Grand Cru (top, only 4% of output)
5.keyPoints.1: Each denomination limits specific varieties — e.g. Scherwiller / Wolxheim: Riesling only; Blienschwiller / Côtes de Barr: Sylvaner only
5.keyPoints.2: Grand Cru is in principle single-variety and hand-harvested, with a base yield of only 55 hl/ha (about 70% of the base tier)
5.keyPoints.3: Two blending exceptions: Altenberg de Bergheim (Riesling + Pinot Gris + Gewurztraminer) and Kaefferkopf (Gewurztraminer + Riesling + Pinot Gris)
